concepts.title: Pilotage
concepts.explain: Pilotage means navigating by recognizable landmarks such as towns, roads, rail lines, and water features. Compare what you see outside with the chart.
concepts.apply: Pick landmarks that are easy to identify from the air and distinct from nearby features.

concepts.title: Dead reckoning
concepts.explain: Dead reckoning predicts position from a known point using direction, time, and speed. Wind changes the path over the ground.
concepts.apply: Update estimated position and arrival time at every checkpoint instead of trusting the first calculation.

concepts.title: Radio and satellite navigation
concepts.explain: Radio aids and satellites provide electronic position or course information. These supplement, not replace, situational awareness.
concepts.apply: Keep track of where you are even when a moving map is available.

concepts.title: Building cross-country confidence
concepts.explain: A strong VFR navigation plan combines charts, weather, landmarks, timing, heading, fuel, and alternates.
concepts.apply: Ask: Where am I? Where will I be next? What if this plan stops working?

check.question: Which is a defining feature of dead reckoning?
options: Estimating position from course, time and speed
check.explanation: Dead reckoning uses a starting position, planned track, time and speed.

concepts.title: Sectional aeronautical charts
concepts.explain: FAA sectional charts depict terrain, obstructions, airports, radio aids, airspace, and other flight information for VFR pilots.
concepts.apply: Review the legend before making assumptions about a line or symbol.

image.caption: FAA Pilot’s Handbook of Aeronautical Knowledge · Figure 16-1 (illustration crop)

concepts.title: Terminal area charts
concepts.explain: Terminal area charts provide more detailed coverage around busy terminal areas; their chart scale is larger than a sectional’s.
concepts.apply: Choose a chart suitable for the complexity and scale of your route.

concepts.title: World aeronautical charts
concepts.explain: The handbook describes world aeronautical charts for broad-area navigation; pilots should verify current product availability before relying on old chart examples.
concepts.apply: Use current chart products and revision dates for actual flight planning.

concepts.title: Measuring chart distances
concepts.explain: Measure along the planned ground track and use the proper chart scale, not the width of a printed page after resizing.
concepts.apply: A route with turns needs the length of each leg summed, not the straight-line distance.

concepts.title: Reading terrain and obstacles
concepts.explain: Terrain elevation, obstacles, and minimum safe altitudes need deliberate scrutiny, especially near high ground.
concepts.apply: Choose an altitude that provides terrain clearance, complies with airspace rules, and fits the aircraft’s performance.

check.question: What does a sectional chart help a VFR pilot identify?
check.explanation: Sectionals combine many geographic and aeronautical details.

concepts.title: Parallels of latitude
concepts.explain: Latitude is measured north or south of the equator. Parallels stay roughly east–west.
concepts.apply: Use latitude together with longitude; a single coordinate alone cannot locate a point.

concepts.title: Meridians of longitude
concepts.explain: Longitude is measured east or west of the prime meridian. Meridians converge at the poles.
concepts.apply: Coordinate entries require the proper hemispheres and format.

image.caption: FAA Pilot’s Handbook of Aeronautical Knowledge · Figure 16-4 (illustration crop)

concepts.title: Minutes and nautical miles
concepts.explain: One minute of latitude corresponds to one nautical mile, approximately, along a meridian. This is useful when measuring distances on charts.
concepts.apply: Measure against the correct latitude scale on your chart.

concepts.title: UTC and time zones
concepts.explain: Aviation commonly uses Coordinated Universal Time to avoid ambiguity across time zones and daylight saving changes.
concepts.apply: Convert forecast and flight-plan times carefully; never guess the UTC offset.

check.question: One minute of latitude is approximately…
check.explanation: A nautical mile is defined from one minute of arc of latitude in the traditional navigation model.

concepts.title: Course
concepts.explain: Course is the intended direction of travel over the ground. Pilots plot course on a chart.
concepts.apply: Plan the route over the ground rather than pointing the nose straight at the destination.

concepts.title: Heading
concepts.explain: Heading is the direction the aircraft nose points. In crosswind, it may differ from ground track.
concepts.apply: A wind correction angle can make heading different from desired course.

concepts.title: Track
concepts.explain: Track is the path actually made over the ground. An aircraft can have a steady heading while its track drifts.
concepts.apply: Compare GPS track or landmarks with desired course to notice drift.

concepts.title: True vs magnetic reference
concepts.explain: True directions reference geographic north; magnetic directions reference magnetic north. State which you are using.
concepts.apply: Avoid mixing a true course with a magnetic heading as though they used the same reference.

concepts.title: Chart plotting
concepts.explain: Use a plotter to find true course between landmarks and to measure each leg.
concepts.apply: Write the course and distance in the navigation log alongside each checkpoint.

check.question: With a crosswind, heading and track…
check.explanation: Wind can move the aircraft sideways over the ground.

concepts.title: Magnetic variation
concepts.explain: Variation is the angular difference between true north and magnetic north; it depends on geographic location.
concepts.apply: Consult charted magnetic information appropriate to the route and chart currency.

concepts.title: East and west variation
concepts.explain: For the common true-to-magnetic conversion, subtract easterly variation and add westerly variation.
concepts.apply: True course 090° with 10°E variation gives magnetic course 080°.

concepts.title: Compass deviation
concepts.explain: Deviation is compass error caused by magnetic influences within the particular aircraft.
concepts.apply: Check the aircraft’s compass correction card; another aircraft’s values do not apply.

concepts.title: Conversions in sequence
concepts.explain: Distinguish true course, true heading, magnetic heading, and compass heading. Wind correction and magnetic errors are separate steps.
concepts.apply: Write each intermediate number and label it, rather than doing several signed changes mentally.

concepts.title: Worked example
concepts.explain: If the true heading is 100° and variation is 8°W, magnetic heading is approximately 108° before any compass deviation.
concepts.apply: The correct final compass reading depends on aircraft-specific deviation.

check.question: True heading 100°, variation 8°W. Magnetic heading is…
check.explanation: For west variation, add 8° going from true to magnetic.

concepts.title: Airspeed vs groundspeed
concepts.explain: True airspeed is speed through the air mass. Groundspeed is movement over Earth and depends on wind.
concepts.apply: Fuel planning and ETA use groundspeed, not just airspeed.

concepts.title: Headwind and tailwind
concepts.explain: A headwind lowers groundspeed; a tailwind raises it, for the same true airspeed, if the wind is aligned with the route.
concepts.apply: At 100 kt TAS and a 20 kt direct headwind, groundspeed is about 80 kt.

concepts.title: Crosswind drift
concepts.explain: Crosswind pushes the aircraft sideways, so pilots point the nose somewhat into wind to maintain the planned track.
concepts.apply: Identify drift by checking ground landmarks against the course line.

image.caption: FAA Pilot’s Handbook of Aeronautical Knowledge · Figure 16-13 (illustration crop)

concepts.title: Wind correction angle
concepts.explain: Wind correction angle is the heading offset needed to counter crosswind drift. Its size depends on wind and airspeed.
concepts.apply: A stronger crosswind generally calls for more correction, other things equal.

concepts.title: Wind triangle
concepts.explain: The wind triangle represents the vector relationship among aircraft motion through air, wind motion, and ground track.
concepts.apply: Use a flight computer or approved electronic calculation to solve crosswind and groundspeed for real flights.

check.question: 100 kt TAS and a direct 20 kt headwind produces about…
check.explanation: A direct headwind subtracts from airspeed when calculating groundspeed.

concepts.title: Time = distance ÷ groundspeed
concepts.explain: For a constant-speed leg, time in hours equals distance in nautical miles divided by groundspeed in knots.
concepts.apply: 60 NM at 120 kt groundspeed requires 0.5 hr, or 30 minutes.

concepts.title: Distance = speed × time
concepts.explain: Distance in NM equals groundspeed in kt multiplied by elapsed time in hours.
concepts.apply: At 90 kt for 20 minutes, distance is approximately 30 NM.

concepts.title: Fuel burn
concepts.explain: Estimated en route fuel equals time multiplied by planned fuel flow, plus required reserves and allowances.
concepts.apply: At 8 gallons per hour for 1.5 hr, cruise consumption is 12 gallons, before other flight phases and reserves.

concepts.title: Revised estimates
concepts.explain: Unexpected wind changes groundspeed and fuel margin even if the airplane’s indicated speed remains the same.
concepts.apply: Recalculate when arrival times differ from the flight log.

concepts.title: Aircraft-specific performance
concepts.explain: The FAA handbook points pilots to the AFM/POH for valid performance inputs and operational limits.
concepts.apply: Use aircraft- and condition-specific numbers rather than example figures in a learning exercise.

check.question: At 120 kt groundspeed, how long is a 60 NM leg?

concepts.title: The E6B
concepts.explain: Mechanical E6B flight computers combine circular slide-rule calculations with a wind side for solving headings and groundspeeds.
concepts.apply: Learn what each input represents rather than copying dial movements blindly.

concepts.title: Electronic flight computers
concepts.explain: Electronic tools calculate similar quantities but still require accurate wind, airspeed, and route inputs.
concepts.apply: Cross-check the result for physical plausibility.

concepts.title: Solving the wind triangle
concepts.explain: Known true course, true airspeed and forecast wind can yield a true heading and predicted groundspeed.
concepts.apply: Calculate each route leg separately if wind direction or altitude changes.

concepts.title: Forecast uncertainty
concepts.explain: Forecast winds are estimates; real wind often differs, especially across altitudes and along terrain.
concepts.apply: Monitor actual groundspeed and modify ETA and fuel estimates in flight.

concepts.title: A cross-check habit
concepts.explain: After any calculation, ask whether the predicted correction points into the wind and whether a headwind reduces groundspeed.
concepts.apply: Direction errors are often caught by simple reality checks.

check.question: Which result is a useful wind-triangle output?
check.explanation: Wind triangle calculations combine aircraft airspeed and wind to determine ground track behavior.

title: Putting Together a VFR Flight Plan

concepts.title: Choose checkpoints
concepts.explain: Select unmistakable checkpoints at practical intervals; avoid features that look nearly identical.
concepts.apply: Prominent rivers, highways, lakes, and towns can make strong visual references.

concepts.title: Route and terrain
concepts.explain: Plot a route considering terrain, obstacles, airspace, weather, emergency landing options, and aircraft performance.
concepts.apply: A straight line is not automatically the safest VFR route.

image.caption: FAA Pilot’s Handbook of Aeronautical Knowledge · Figure 16-25 (illustration crop)

concepts.title: Altitude selection
concepts.explain: Select altitude compatible with terrain clearance, airspace, cloud clearances, aircraft performance and applicable cruising altitude rules.
concepts.apply: Consider winds aloft and visibility alongside terrain.

concepts.title: Nav log
concepts.explain: A navigation log records course, headings, distances, groundspeed, estimated time, fuel and frequencies.
concepts.apply: Update it from actual checkpoint passage times and actual conditions.

concepts.title: Flight plan and services
concepts.explain: Filing a VFR flight plan is distinct from obtaining ATC flight following; opening and closing a flight plan require attention.
concepts.apply: Know which service you requested and whether your plan is actually activated.

concepts.title: Aircraft readiness
concepts.explain: Performance and weight-and-balance checks must agree with the aircraft-specific AFM/POH.
concepts.apply: A well-plotted route is not safe if the aircraft cannot depart or climb as assumed.

check.question: Which item belongs in a VFR navigation log?
options: Checkpoint distances and estimated leg times
check.explanation: Nav logs help monitor course, timing, fuel and progress.

concepts.title: VHF line of sight
concepts.explain: VHF navigation signals behave largely as line of sight; terrain and low altitude can limit reception.
concepts.apply: Do not assume a ground station is receivable behind a mountain.

concepts.title: VOR basics
concepts.explain: A VOR provides magnetic radials from a ground facility. A radial identifies direction FROM that facility.
concepts.apply: The 090 radial extends east from the station; it does not mean the airplane is heading east.

concepts.title: Station identification
concepts.explain: Identify the tuned navigation facility using its published identifier and correct frequency.
concepts.apply: A needle indication is not meaningful if you are tuned to the wrong station.

concepts.title: Service volume
concepts.explain: Published service volumes and NOTAMs affect reliability and availability.
concepts.apply: Use current navigation information rather than expecting reception everywhere.

concepts.title: Course indications
concepts.explain: The course deviation indicator shows displacement relative to a selected course, subject to correct setting and instrument context.
concepts.apply: Interpret TO/FROM separately from left/right displacement.

check.question: What does the VOR 090 radial indicate?
options: A line east FROM the station
A line west FROM the station
check.explanation: VOR radials are referenced as magnetic bearings outward from the VOR.

concepts.title: Omnibearing selector (OBS)
concepts.explain: On a conventional VOR indicator, the OBS selects the course to be displayed. The CDI needle then shows lateral deviation relative to it.
concepts.apply: Set the intended course before interpreting CDI deflection.

concepts.title: TO/FROM indication
concepts.explain: The flag helps indicate whether the selected course generally points toward or away from the station. It does not independently prove a safe heading.
concepts.apply: Combine the flag with your known position and selected course.

concepts.title: Radial interception
concepts.explain: Use an intercept heading to join a desired course, then turn to a wind-corrected tracking heading.
concepts.apply: Avoid chasing CDI movements with large, uncontrolled heading changes.

concepts.title: Station passage
concepts.explain: Near station passage, VOR indications can fluctuate; anticipate the zone of confusion.
concepts.apply: Cross-check with timing and other navigation indications.

concepts.title: HSI and RMI
concepts.explain: HSIs and RMIs present directional information in different formats; understand your installed display before relying on it.
concepts.apply: Train on the specific equipment in the aircraft, especially overlay modes.

image.caption: FAA Pilot’s Handbook of Aeronautical Knowledge · Figure 16-30 (illustration crop)

check.question: A VOR radial describes a bearing…
check.explanation: Radials are defined outward from the ground facility.

concepts.title: Distance measuring equipment
concepts.explain: DME gives slant-range distance to the ground station, which can exceed horizontal ground distance.
concepts.apply: Near a station at altitude, DME may show a nonzero value even if directly overhead.

concepts.title: Time-to-station estimation
concepts.explain: The handbook describes using CDI bearing change and time to estimate time/distance to a VOR.
concepts.apply: This is an approximation requiring stable heading and groundspeed.

concepts.title: RNAV concepts
concepts.explain: Area navigation lets an aircraft navigate between selected points instead of flying only directly station-to-station.
concepts.apply: Check database validity, sensor availability, and the installed equipment’s limitations.

concepts.title: Where the signal comes from
concepts.explain: Traditional radio RNAV may combine VOR/DME signals; modern area navigation often relies on GNSS.
concepts.apply: Do not assume every RNAV panel has the same underlying sensor or capability.

concepts.title: Redundancy
concepts.explain: Navigation decisions should account for failures, signal anomalies, and how to continue safely.
concepts.apply: Keep an alternative means of position awareness.

check.question: Why can DME differ from map distance?
check.explanation: DME measures straight-line distance between aircraft and station.

concepts.title: NDB and ADF
concepts.explain: An NDB transmits nondirectional radio signals; an ADF receiver indicates the direction to the signal source relative to the aircraft.
concepts.apply: Check which bearing the installed ADF instrument actually displays.

concepts.title: Relative bearing
concepts.explain: Relative bearing is measured clockwise from the aircraft nose to the station, from 000° to 359°.
concepts.apply: An indicated relative bearing of 090° means the station is to your right.

concepts.title: Magnetic bearing
concepts.explain: For a fixed-card ADF, magnetic bearing to station equals magnetic heading plus relative bearing, normalized within 360°.
concepts.apply: At heading 030° and relative bearing 090°, bearing TO station is 120°.

concepts.title: ADF limitations
concepts.explain: Lightning, night effects, terrain, and coastal refraction may degrade ADF reliability.
concepts.apply: Treat a rapidly changing needle cautiously in convective weather.

concepts.title: Tracking vs homing
concepts.explain: Homing continuously points toward a station and may curve in crosswind. Tracking uses wind correction to maintain a desired ground path.
concepts.apply: A straight plotted track generally requires drift correction.

check.question: Magnetic heading 030°, ADF relative bearing 090°. Bearing TO station?
check.explanation: Add 30° and 90° for a magnetic bearing of 120°.

concepts.title: Satellite ranging
concepts.explain: GPS estimates receiver position from satellite signals and accurate timing. Geometry and signal quality influence accuracy.
concepts.apply: A position display is not proof of integrity under all conditions.

image.caption: FAA Pilot’s Handbook of Aeronautical Knowledge · Figure 16-40 (illustration crop)

concepts.title: Database and waypoints
concepts.explain: A GPS waypoint uses defined coordinates; airport, intersection, or user waypoint labels must be entered correctly.
concepts.apply: Verify the waypoint identifier and displayed location before activating direct-to.

concepts.title: Receiver limitations
concepts.explain: Not all GPS receivers or installations are approved for the same uses. Handheld VFR receivers are supplemental.
concepts.apply: Follow the AFM/POH supplement and applicable approval requirements.

concepts.title: RAIM and integrity
concepts.explain: Some IFR-approved receivers use integrity-monitoring features such as RAIM. Availability varies by equipment and constellation.
concepts.apply: Read equipment-specific annunciations and limitations rather than relying on a generic rule.

concepts.title: Automation awareness
concepts.explain: The correct map display can still show an unsafe route through weather, airspace or terrain.
concepts.apply: Continuously cross-check situational awareness outside and with current information.

concepts.title: Lost GPS procedures
concepts.explain: Treat GPS failure as a navigation contingency: use chart, pilotage, dead reckoning, and available ground-based aids.
concepts.apply: Never let a failed display become a loss of basic navigation capability.

check.question: Which check is essential after entering a GPS waypoint?
options: Assume matching letters always mean the desired point
check.explanation: Similar waypoint identifiers can cause wrong-waypoint navigation errors.

concepts.title: Recognize being uncertain
concepts.explain: If visual landmarks do not match the expected route, acknowledge uncertainty promptly rather than continuing blindly.
concepts.apply: Climb if safe and appropriate for reception/visibility and terrain, check fuel, and establish position.

concepts.title: The classic five Cs
concepts.explain: The common lost-pilot memory aid is climb, communicate, confess, comply and conserve; actual actions depend on conditions.
concepts.apply: Ask ATC or Flight Service for help while preserving terrain and airspace safety.

concepts.title: Diversion planning
concepts.explain: A diversion begins with a reachable alternate, approximate heading, distance, fuel, runway suitability and weather.
concepts.apply: In an emergency, prioritize immediate safe navigation before precise paperwork or chart plotting.

concepts.title: Reassess fuel and daylight
concepts.explain: Uncertainty, headwinds, and detours consume fuel and daylight margins.
concepts.apply: Make a conservative diversion early rather than preserving the original plan at all costs.

concepts.title: Task prioritization
concepts.explain: Aviate, navigate, communicate: keep control and collision avoidance ahead of elaborate calculations.
concepts.apply: Use all available resources and declare an emergency when necessary.

check.question: While lost or diverting, the first priority is to…
check.explanation: Aviate first; plan navigation and communication without compromising aircraft control.

concepts.title: Prepare the chart
concepts.explain: Mark a safe route, current chart symbols, prominent checkpoints and alternates.
concepts.apply: Can you locate plausible alternatives on either side of the route?

concepts.title: Prepare headings
concepts.explain: Measure true course, solve expected wind correction and convert to magnetic/compass as necessary.
concepts.apply: Record the reference north for every direction.

concepts.title: Prepare leg times
concepts.explain: Estimate groundspeed, leg time, fuel flow, fuel requirements and reserves using aircraft data.
concepts.apply: Build a margin for forecast and operational uncertainty.

concepts.title: Conduct in-flight checks
concepts.explain: Verify progress over each checkpoint, update time and fuel, and monitor weather and airspace.
concepts.apply: Treat unexplained ETA change as a reason to reassess wind and navigation.

concepts.title: Handle an unexpected headwind
concepts.explain: A slower-than-expected groundspeed increases travel time and fuel use.
concepts.apply: Compute updated range to a diversion airport before fuel margins become critical.

concepts.title: Make a safe decision
concepts.explain: Safety overrides completing the original itinerary. A diversion is an ordinary, professional response to deteriorating conditions.
concepts.apply: Choose an alternate early when weather, fuel, or confidence is insufficient.

check.question: Actual groundspeed drops below the planned value. What should you do?
options: Maintain ETA by flying beyond aircraft limits
check.explanation: Slower groundspeed increases time en route and fuel use, potentially calling for diversion.
